transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-05-21 15:00 UTC | Duration: 1:02 | Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Sanjay Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (Skylark - Head of ML), Tom Bennett (Skylark - SRE), Priya Kapoor (Skylark - Product), Eli Zhang (Skylark - ML Eng)

Auto-generated summary: Quick POC scoping to align on benchmark harness integration, discuss customer scripts, streaming vs non-streaming runs, success criteria (latency/cost), and schedule a pilot load test. Agreed to exchange artifacts and schedule a 2-hour run.

[00:00] Laura Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro - I'm Laura, AE on the Redwood platform, and Sanjay here is our SE who will run the harness and the bench tests.
[00:12] Sanjay Patel: hi all, quick wave. I put a quick agenda in the calendar: understand the workload, get the scripts, decide streaming vs non-streaming for the harness, and agree success criteria and timelines.
[00:22] Maya Ortiz: thanks, Laura. from Skylark's side... I'm Maya, head of ML. we want to validate end-to-end latency under load for our summarization pipeline and measure cost per 1M tokens so we can decide whether to go Dedicated vs Hosted.
[00:35] Tom Bennett: Tom here, SRE. i care about sustained throughput, network egress, and that the harness can run inside our VPC.
[00:45] Priya Kapoor: Priya, product — timeline is important. we want results before our Q3 planning cut-off so, end of June ideally.
[00:55] Sanjay Patel: great. quick clarifying q: is your inference path streaming token-by-token to clients, or do you batch and return full responses?
[01:05] Eli Zhang: we actually have both. the real-time UI uses streaming for the user-facing side, and an async job runs bulk summarization non-streaming. most of the heavy load for value is the async jobs but the UI latency matters for NPS.
[01:18] Laura Chen: good, so we should plan two benchmark profiles: a streaming profile that measures tail latency and reassembly overhead, and a batch/non-streaming profile focused on throughput and cost per token.
[01:28] Maya Ortiz: yeah and token lengths vary — UI calls average 120 tokens, async jobs average 2k tokens with a long-tail to 8k sometimes.
[01:38] Sanjay Patel: perfect — please send over token distribution CSV. that helps the harness pick seq-lens and warmup behavior. On the harness side we support streaming via chunked HTTP and gRPC-ish streaming; we can replay customer scripts as-is or adapt them into Locust/JMeter drivers.
[01:51] Tom Bennett: speaking of replay, our current scripts are python clients built on top of openai-client like wrappers with some custom retry logic. can you run those directly or do we need to convert?
[02:02] Sanjay Patel: we can run python-based harnesses directly. best practice is to provide a small wrapper that emits the same timing semantics (think think-time, client-side batching). if you include your retry policy we can simulate user behavior more accurately.
[02:16] Priya Kapoor: important for our stakeholders: what are realistic success criteria? we talked internally about p50 < 120ms for UI and p95 < 600ms for streaming; for async p95 under 10s and cost under $7 per 1M tokens. are those feasible?
[02:30] Sanjay Patel: initial sanity check: p50 120ms for UI is ambitious depending on model and region; if you're on a hosted shared tier latency will be higher. on Dedicated or private deployment with A100/H100 approximations, p50 ~80-140ms is achievable for small seq lengths and smaller models. p95 tail depends heavily on batching and cache warmup.
[02:49] Laura Chen: also need to define accuracy/regression checks during the POC — we can run a small eval set of prompts to ensure quantization or routing doesn't change outputs beyond your threshold.
[03:01] Maya Ortiz: we will share a 200-example eval set with pass/fail tolerances.
[03:06] Sanjay Patel: excellent. on the bench config: we recommend three phases — 1) functional replay (sanity), 2) ramp and soak (sustained throughput), 3) stress/peak burst test. each phase will publish p50/p90/p95, tokens/sec, GPU util, and cost estimate.
[03:21] Eli Zhang: how do you estimate cost? we need to report expected monthly spend for both Hosted and Dedicated scenarios.
[03:26] Sanjay Patel: we run unit economics using tokens/sec * tokens per request * price per token per GPU-hour mapping. for Dedicated we model reserved cores and amortized infra. we'll produce a markdown breakdown in the report.
[03:36] Tom Bennett: networking — we need the harness to be able to run from our VPC, also capture egress numbers. can you support an on-prem runner?
[03:44] Sanjay Patel: yes, we have a lightweight runner (docker image) that can be deployed in customer env; it streams metrics back to the Redwood console over an encrypted channel, or you can keep metrics local and share CSVs. for air-gapped we can do offline artifact exchange.
[03:58] Priya Kapoor: in terms of infra, what GPUs were you expecting to validate with? we listed A100 and H100 in the RFP — any quantization differences matter?
[04:07] Sanjay Patel: H100 tends to be faster for fp16 and some newer kernels, A100 is predictable. quantization (4-bit/8-bit) changes latency and quality; we will run both full-fp16 and quantized variants if you want. we'll also surface recommended kernel flags and batch sizes.
[04:23] Maya Ortiz: when you run streaming tests, how do you measure reassembly latency and client-perceived latency?
[04:29] Sanjay Patel: harness will emit two metrics: server token latency (server-side token emission time) and client reassembly delta (time from first server byte to reconstructed response). for chunked HTTP we measure chunk sizes and reassembly overhead.
[04:42] Laura Chen: small note: some transcriptions of our product in the past had names wrong — Redwood runtime sometimes appears as Redwood inference engine or just "runtime"; ignore small naming mismatches in notes.
[04:51] Tom Bennett: fair. one of our concerns is deterministic warm-up and KV cache priming — for batch jobs cache behavior leads to big differences in p95. can your harness prime KV cache?
[04:59] Sanjay Patel: yes. we support controlled priming sequences; we can replay recent prefixes to warm the KV cache and measure cold vs warm p95s. we'll log cache hit rates as well.
[05:12] Eli Zhang: for the async jobs, we have multi-document concatenation which produces long-context behavior and sometimes causes OOM on smaller GPUs. can you model memory utilization?
[05:20] Sanjay Patel: we collect GPU memory curves and OOM events; we'll include memory footprint per sequence length run. if we hit OOM, we'll suggest quantization or request sharding strategies.
[05:31] Maya Ortiz: about the harness itself — do you have an existing repo we can fork or a private link?
[05:36] Laura Chen: yes, I'll share the benchmark harness repo (public-private link) with a README and example python drivers. It'll include templates for streaming (chunked HTTP) and non-streaming (batched RPC), plus a docker runner.
[05:48] Priya Kapoor: would you also send an example report template so our execs can review results quickly?
[05:52] Sanjay Patel: yes, the report template includes latency percentiles, throughput, GPU utilization, cost breakdown, and a verdict: go/no-go per success criteria.
[05:59] Tom Bennett: what about monitoring during the run — do you stream traces to your console or can we integrate with our Prometheus?
[06:06] Sanjay Patel: we emit Prometheus metrics via a push gateway if you want. for the POC we'll enable both: internal metrics and a short-lived Prom push for your SREs.
[06:15] Maya Ortiz: ok timeline recap?
[06:18] Laura Chen: recap - Laura shares repo + quickstart by 2025-05-23; Skylark sends canonical scripts + sample data by 2025-05-26; Sanjay prepares harness templates by 2025-05-24; Tom provisions VPC creds by 2025-05-25. We target a 2-hour run week of 2025-05-26 and a follow-up postmortem the next business day.
[06:35] Priya Kapoor: sounds good. one last Q — are there any licensing or security checklist items to review before we run in our VPC?
[06:42] Laura Chen: we'll share the security summary: SOC 2 compliance attestation, encryption in transit, KMS integration notes. for VPC runner we have a short checklist around outbound ports and token rotation.
[06:53] Maya Ortiz: perfect. thanks everyone.
[06:56] Sanjay Patel: thanks, I'll draft the test plan and share with Maya and Tom.
[06:59] Laura Chen: great — talk soon. bye.

Post-meeting notes: planned benchmarks: streaming UI profile, async batch profile, cold vs warm cache, quantized vs fp16 comparisons. Deliverables: harness link, example drivers, report template, scheduled 2-hour run.
